text: 10 Lecture 10 10.1 Characteristic polynomial Lemma 10.1. Let T : V → V be a linear transformation, v ∈ V an eigenvector of T with eigenvalue λ i.e. T v = λv. Let β, γ be two bases of V A[v]β = λ[v]β T v = λv B[v]γ = λ[v]γ B = P −1AP [v]β = P [v]γ A=[T ]β β B=[T ]γ γ We have pB(x) = pA(x). We can define pT (x) = pA(x) where A = [T ] β β. Proof. If T v = λv, then [T ]β β[v]β = [T (v)]β = λ[v]β. pP AP −1(x) = det(xI − P −1AP ) = det(P −1(xI − A)P ) = det(xI − A) = pA(x). Proposition 10.2. The characteristic polynomial is of the form pA(x) = xn − c1(A)xn−1 + · · · + (−1) ncn(A) where ck(A) is some function of A for example, c1(A) = tr(A) = a11 + a22 + · · · + ann and cn(A) = det(A). For any P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible, we have pA(x) = pP AP −1(x). In particular ck(P −1AP ) = ck(A). If pA(x) = (x − λ1) · · · (x − λn) splits in F , then ck(A) = ∑ i1<···<ik λi1 · · · λik . Proof. Note that (xI − A)ij = xδij − aij. By the Leibniz formula of the determinant (Theorem 8.1) pA(x) = det(xI − A) = ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)(xδσ(1)1 − aσ(1)1) · · · (xδσ(n)n − aσ(n)n). It is clear that (−1)ncn(A) = pA(0) = det(−A) = (−1)n det(A). Therefore, cn(A) = det(A). To find the coefficient of xn, we observe that the right hand side is the sum of products of n factors of degree ≤ 1. The only term that can contribute xn is the one where there is an x in each factor. This is only possible when σ(i) = i for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n, i.e. σ = id. Note that sign(id) = 1 and so this term is (x − a11) · · · (x − ann). Thus we see that the coefficient of xn is 1. To find the coefficient of xn−1, we observe that the term that contribute xn−1 should have an x in at least n − 1 factors. This means σ(i) = i for all but one 1 ≤ i ≤ n. However, since σ : {1, . . . , n} → {1, . . . , n} is bijective, we must have σ(i) = i for all 56 1 ≤ i ≤ n. The term that contributes xn−1 is (x−a11) · · · (x−ann) again. The coefficient of xn−1 is −a11 − · · · − ann = − tr(A). Suppose pA(x) = (x − λ1) · · · (x − λn) We now expand the product. To obtain the coefficient of xn−k, we must choose the term x from exactly (n − k) of the factors, and choose the term −λi from the remaining k factors. Any such choice contributes (−1)kλi1 · · · λik . Since each k-tuple of distinct indices {i1, . . . , ik} ⊂ {1, . . . , n} occurs exactly once in the expansion, the coefficient of xn−k is (−1) k ∑ i1<···<ik λi1 · · · λik . Comparing coefficients with xn − c1(A)xn−1 + · · · + (−1)ncn(A) we get ck(A) = ∑ i1<···<ik λi1 · · · λik . . Example 10.3. A = ( 7 −10 5 −8 ) , tr(A) = 7 − 8 = −1, det(A) = 7(−8) − 5(−10) = −6. Thus pA(x) = x2 + x − 6. On the other hand, P −1AP = diag(−3, 2) and tr(A) = −3 + 2, det(A) = (−3)(2) = −6. Remark 10.4. There is a formula for ck(A) in terms of the entries of A which is the sum of principal k-minors of A. For a definition of principal k-minors and a proof of the formula, see here. Corollary 10.5. A ∈ Mn×n(F ) has at most n eigenvalues counting multiplicity. In other words, (λI − A) is invertible for all but at most n values of λ ∈ F . Proposition 10.6. We have the following properties of the trace map. (i) tr : Mn×n(F ) → F is a linear function. (ii) Let A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then we have tr(AB) = tr(BA). Remark 10.7. (ii) is stronger than tr(P −1AP ) = tr(A). Remark 10.8. If A, B, C ∈ Mn×n(F ), then by (ii) we have tr(ABC) = tr(CAB) = tr(BCA). However, in general tr(ABC) ̸= tr(BAC). Proof. (i) This is clear from definition. (ii) Let A = (aij) and B = (bij). By the definition of matrix multiplication, (AB)ii = n∑ k=1 aikbki. Therefore, tr(AB) = n∑ i=1(AB)ii = n∑ i=1 n∑ k=1 aikbki. 57 We may interchange the order of summation: tr(AB) = n∑ k=1 n∑ i=1 aikbki = n∑ k=1 n∑ i=1 bkiaik. But this is exactly: tr(BA) = n∑ k=1(BA)kk = n∑ k=1 n∑ i=1 bkiaik. Hence, tr(AB) = tr(BA). 10.2 Diagonalizability Theorem 10.9. Let λ1, . . . , λm be distinct eigenvalues of A ∈ Mn×n(F ). Let vi be an eigenvector corresponding to λi for 1 ≤ i ≤ m. Then v1, . . . , vm are linearly independent. In particular E(λ1, A) + · · · + E(λm, A) = E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λm, A) and if βi is a basis of E(λi, A), then β = β1 ∪ · · · ∪ βm is a basis of E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λm, A). Proof. We prove by induction on m. If m = 1, then v1 ̸= 0. Hence v1 is linearly independent. Suppose the conclusion is true for m − 1, we now prove it for m. Let a1, . . . , am ∈ F be such that a1v1 + · · · + amvm = 0. (2) Applying T on both sides and using they are eigenvalues, we get a1λ1v1 + · · · + amλmvm = 0. (3) Multiplying λm on both sides of (2) we have a1λmv1 + · · · + amλmvm = 0. (4) Subtracting (4) from (3), we get a1(λ1 − λm)v1 + · · · + am−1(λm−1 − λm)vm−1 = 0. By induction hypothesis, v1, . . . , vm−1 are linearly independent. Thus ai(λi − λm) = 0 for 1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1. Since λi are distinct, we have ai = 0 for 1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1. Plugging back into (2), we get amvm = 0. Since vm ̸= 0, we have am = 0. We now show that E(λ1, A)+· · ·+E(λm, A) = E(λ1, A)⊕· · ·⊕E(λm, A). If this is not true, then by Proposition 3.5, there are wi ∈ E(λi, A) for 1 ≤ i ≤ m with some wi ̸= 0 such that 0 = w1 + · · · + wm. Let w1, . . . , wr be all nonzero wi’s. Then w1 + · · · + wr = 0. This contradicts the fact that w1, . . . , wr are linearly independent. Let βi = (v(i) 1 , · · · , v(i) ki ) be a basis of E(λi, A). Then we would like to show that β = (v(1) 1 , · · · , v(1) k1 , . . . , v(m) 1 , · · · , v(m) km ) are linearly independent. Let a(i) l ∈ F be such that m∑ i=1 ki∑ l=1 a(i) l v(i) l = 0. 58 Then with wi = ∑ki l=1 a (i) l v(i) l , we have w1 +· · ·+wm = 0. Since E(λ1, A)⊕· · ·⊕E(λm, A) is a direct sum, wi = ∑ki l=1 a(i) l v(i) l = 0. Since βi is a basis, we have a (i) l = 0 for any 1 ≤ i ≤ m, 1 ≤ l ≤ ki. Proposition 10.10. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) and λ ∈ F be an eigenvalue of A. Then we have the geometric multiplicity of λ ≤ the algebraic multiplicity of λ. Proof. Since λ is an eigenvalue of A, we have the geometric multiplicity m = dim E(λ, A) ≥ 1. Let v1, . . . , vm ∈ F n be a basis of E(λ, A). We extend v1, . . . , vm to a basis β = (v1, . . . , vn) of V = F n. Let P be the matrix whose columns are v1, . . . , vn since vi ∈ F n are column vectors. (Or one can say P is the change of basis matrix from the standard basis to β.) We would like to find P −1AP . Since Avi = λvi for i = 1, . . . , m and Avj is unknown for m + 1 ≤ j ≤ n, we have P −1AP = ( λIm B 0 C ) . Then by Proposition 9.3 pA(x) =pP −1AP (x) = det ( xIm − λIm −B 0 xIn−m − C ) = det((x − λ)Im) det(xIn−m − C) = (x − λ) mpC(x). In particular, (x − λ)m | pA(x). By definition of algebraic multiplicity, m ≤ algebraic multiplicity of λ. Theorem 10.11. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then the following are equivalent. (i) A is diagonalizable over F (ii) pA splits over F and geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity for each eigenvalue. (iii) n = dim E(λ1, A) + · · · + dim E(λm, A) (iv) F n = E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λm, A) Proof. (i) =⇒ (ii) If A is diagonalizable, then P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn). Then pA(x) = pP −1AP (x) = det(xI −diag(λ1, . . . , λn)) = (x−λ1) · · · (x−λn). For each λi, the algebraic multiplicity of λi is the number of times ki that λi appear in diag(λ1, . . . , λn). The corresponding columns of P are linearly independent eigenvectors of eigenvalue λi. Thus the algebraic multiplicity ki is equal to dim E(λi, A) which is the geometric multiplicity. (ii) =⇒ (iii) Since pA(x) splits in F , we have pA(x) = (x − λ1) k1(x − λ2) k2 · · · (x − λm)km where λi are distinct roots of pA(x). Since geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity, we have dim E(λi, A) = ki. Since deg pA = n, we have n = k1+· · ·+km = dim E(λ1, A)+ · · · + dim E(λm, A). 59 (iii) =⇒ (iv) By Theorem 10.9, (iii), Proposition 3.5 and Corollary 2.17, we have F n = E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λm, A). (iv) =⇒ (i) Let βi be a basis of E(λi, A). By Theorem 10.9, β = β1 ∪· · ·∪βm is a basis of E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λm, A) = F n. Thus we have a basis consisting of eigenvectors. Corollary 10.12. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). If A has n distinct eigenvalues in F , then A is diagonalizable. Proof. For any eigenvalue λi, we have dim E(λi, A) ≥ 1. Then we have n ≥ dim(E(λ1, A) + · · · + E(λn, A)) = dim(E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λn, A)) = dim E(λ1, A) + · · · + dim E(λn, A) ≥ n. Thus equality holds and we have A is diagonalizable. 10.3 Cayley-Hamilton theorem Definition 10.13. Let T : V → V be a linear transformation on a vector space over F . Let p(x) = anxn + · · · + a0 ∈ F [x]. Then we define f (T ) = anT n + an−1T n−1 + · · · + a1T + a0id. Note that f (T ) : V → V is also a linear transformation. Similarly, for A ∈ Mn×n(F ), we define f (A) ∈ Mn×n(F ) as f (A) = amAm + am−1Am−1 + · · · + a1A + a0I. Proposition 10.14. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) be fixed. The map F [x] → Mn×n(F ) f (x) ↦→ f (A) preserves polynomial addition and multiplication. That is for f (x), g(x) in F [x] we have (f + g)(A) = f (A) + g(A) and (f g)(A) = f (A)g(A). Proof. Suppose f (x) = ∑m j=0 ajxj and g(x) = ∑m k=0 bkxk. Then (f + g)(x) = m∑ j=0(aj + bj)xj (f g)(x) = m∑ j=0 m∑ k=0 ajbkxj+k. Thus (f + g)(A) = m∑ j=0(aj + bj)Aj = m∑ j=0 ajAj + m∑ j=0 bjAj = f (A) + g(A) (f g)(A) = m∑ j=0 n∑ k=0 ajbkAj+k =   m∑ j=0 ajAj   ( n∑ k=0 bkAk) = f (A)g(A). 60 Lemma 10.15. If B = P −1AP , then f (B) = P −1f (A)P . Proof. Bk = (P −1AP ) · · · (P −1AP ) = P −1AkP f (B)v = anBn + · · · + a0I = anP −1AnP + · · · + a0I = P −1(anAn + · · · + a0I)P = P −1f (A)P . 61
